text.title: Rails Patterns Core Rules
text.summary: 9 testable rules grounding the Service Object + ServiceResult patterns for Rails 7+. Each rule pairs a binary check + sourced rationale.

rule.statement: Exactly one `ServiceResult` class MUST exist at `app/services/service_result.rb`. Its public API MUST be `success?` / `failure?` / `value` / `errors`. CI MUST fail on a second definition or alternate API (`ok?`, `result?`).
rule.rationale: LLMs invent slightly different shapes per file; divergent APIs force controllers to handle every variation.

rule.statement: Service classes MUST accept `params:` and `current_user:` keyword args in `initialize`. The public API MUST be a single `call` instance method returning `ServiceResult`. Helpers MUST be private. Namespacing follows `Users::CreateService`. The service is the unit-of-work boundary: multi-write logic wraps in `ActiveRecord::Base.transaction` inside `call`, and controllers and models MUST NOT open a transaction for a business action.

rationale.source: Internal — service-discoverability retro; Rails guides — Transactions

rule.rationale: Consistent signatures make every service testable + discoverable the same way. Putting the transaction anywhere else blends the HTTP scope (or the record's lifecycle) with the database's, which is what leaves half-written state behind a redirect.

rule.statement: Mail, webhooks, search-index updates MUST run from `after_commit` callbacks, an outbox, or chained Sidekiq jobs. Calling `deliver_later` / external HTTP inside `ActiveRecord::Base.transaction` is forbidden.
rule.rationale: `deliver_later` inside a transaction enqueues before commit; rollback leaves the worker running against a non-existent record.

rule.statement: Controllers MUST call `params.require(...).permit(...)` and pass the permitted hash to the service. Services MUST NOT touch `params`, `request`, or any HTTP global.
rule.rationale: Strong Params enforce the allowlist at the HTTP boundary; passing raw params reintroduces mass-assignment risk.

rule.statement: `ApplicationController` MUST `after_action :verify_authorized` + `after_action :verify_policy_scoped` (Pundit). Every controller action MUST call `authorize @resource` or `policy_scope(Resource)` explicitly.
rule.rationale: Without `verify_authorized`, an agent adding a new action may forget `authorize` and leave it unprotected.

rule.statement: CI MUST run Bullet (N+1), Brakeman (security), bundler-audit (CVEs) on every PR and block merge on any failure.
rule.rationale: Without automated gates, N+1 regressions, SQL-injection patterns, and outdated gem CVEs ship to production.

rule.statement: Each service class MUST encapsulate exactly one business action, named verb-first (`Orders::PlaceOrderService`, `Orders::RefundOrderService`). A class exposing `create` + `update` + `cancel` as public methods is forbidden; so is a service over 150 lines.
rule.rationale: A multi-action service is the fat model relocated — it re-accumulates the same conditionals. One action per class keeps the name honest and the test focused.

rule.statement: `call` MUST signal business failure by returning `ServiceResult.failure(error: :symbol)`. Raising an exception for a business outcome (insufficient stock, payment declined), or returning a naked boolean or `nil`, is forbidden — exceptions are reserved for bugs and infrastructure faults.
rule.rationale: Exceptions as control flow force every caller into a `rescue` and hide the failure set from the reader; an explicit result makes each branch visible at the call site.

rule.statement: Every service MUST have a spec under `spec/services/` that runs without booting the HTTP stack (load `spec_helper`, not `rails_helper`, where possible) and covers each business branch with mocked collaborators. A request spec alone does not satisfy this.

rationale.source: RSpec Rails — request specs vs unit specs

rule.rationale: A service exercised only through HTTP is retested for the controller's reasons, runs an order of magnitude slower, and leaves its failure branches uncovered.
